messages.content: I want to design an ownership type checker for cancellable asynchronous tasks that can safely transfer borrowed resources across task boundaries.

The central goal is to make borrowing across a task boundary compatible with ownership rules even when the task can be cancelled or migrated. The checker should guarantee memory safety in those circumstances without relying on whole-program analysis or runtime borrow checks. It should also accept 12 safe programs and reject 12 unsafe programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation.
Why is crossing a task boundary important here? Isn't a borrow still just a borrow?

It is still a borrow, so its validity depends on the resource remaining available for as long as the borrow can be used. A task boundary matters because the task may continue at a different point in time or execution context from the code that supplied the resource. The checker therefore has to account for the borrow's continued use across that boundary, rather than treating the boundary as if it ended the borrow.
And cancellation adds another possible end to the task?

Yes. Cancellation means ordinary completion cannot be the only situation considered when deciding whether borrowed resources remain safe. The memory-safety guarantee needs to hold if the task is cancelled as well as if it runs normally. That does not, by itself, prescribe a particular cancellation mechanism or say that cancellation must happen at any specific point.
How should I read the task-migration part of the requirement?

Migration means the safety argument cannot depend on the task always staying in the same execution context. A transferred borrow must remain valid under whatever task migration the intended system permits. The goal does not specify a particular scheduler, machine boundary, or migration mechanism; it specifies that migration must not undermine memory safety.
Do cancellation and migration have to be considered together, or can each be handled in isolation?

The stated guarantee is memory safety under cancellation and task migration, so it should not depend on ignoring either one when both are relevant to a task. They are distinct concerns: cancellation changes how execution may end, while migration changes where execution may continue. Neither should make an otherwise invalid use of a borrowed resource appear safe.
What does the restriction against whole-program analysis rule out at a high level?

The guarantee must not require inspecting an entire program before a task and its borrowed resources can be checked. The checker needs a way to establish the necessary ownership and borrowing conditions without depending on knowledge of every use elsewhere in the program. That describes the required scope of the analysis, not a particular checker architecture.
And no runtime borrow checks means the guarantee has to come from the type checker?

Right. Borrow validity should not depend on checking borrowing rules dynamically while the tasks run. The design goal is a static ownership-type-checking guarantee. This restriction is specifically about runtime borrow checks; it does not say that asynchronous tasks require no runtime execution machinery.
I also want to keep borrowing separate from ownership transfer. How do those fit together in the goal?

They are related but not interchangeable. A borrowed resource is usable subject to the borrowing relationship; transferring ownership changes who is entitled to use or dispose of the owned resource. The checker must handle safe transfer of borrowed resources across task boundaries while also distinguishing cases involving ownership transfer. The program set explicitly needs coverage of ownership transfer, but the goal does not prescribe one particular transfer protocol.
What makes nested borrows a meaningful part of the program set?

With nested borrows, the validity of one borrow can depend on another borrowing relationship. A checker cannot assess a use across a task boundary solely by noticing that a resource was borrowed; it must preserve the relevant relationships when deciding whether that use is safe. The requirement is for the accepted and rejected programs to cover nested borrows, without specifying particular nesting depths or syntax.
Can you give a general unsafe shape without claiming it is one of the 12 programs?

As a conceptual illustration, a task using a borrowed resource after that borrow is no longer valid would be unsafe, whether the problematic use arose along a normal path or around cancellation. Likewise, treating an ownership transfer as though the original owner retained an unrestricted right to use the resource would raise an ownership-safety concern. Those are illustrations of what the checker must reason about, not descriptions of any designated test program.
What would a safe shape look like at the same level of generality?

Conceptually, a task could use a transferred borrow while its validity is maintained throughout every permitted use, including the possibilities relevant to cancellation and migration. If ownership is transferred, subsequent uses would have to respect that transfer. The point of accepting safe programs is that the checker should permit uses for which those obligations hold, rather than rejecting every task that carries a borrow.
So accepting safe programs matters as much as identifying dangerous ones?

Both are explicit requirements. The checker must accept 12 safe programs and reject 12 unsafe programs. Rejecting everything involving a cross-task borrow would not satisfy the acceptance requirement, even if it avoided unsafe executions. Conversely, accepting the safe programs is not enough if the unsafe ones pass the checker.
Are those 12 safe and 12 unsafe programs required separately for each of nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation?

No such per-category count is stated. The numerical requirement is 12 accepted safe programs and 12 rejected unsafe programs, with the programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation. That gives 24 programs in the specified set, but it does not say how many must fall into each topic or whether a program may cover more than one.
Would a design that handles cancellation but assumes tasks never migrate meet the goal?

Not as stated. Memory safety must hold under task migration as well as cancellation. A safety argument that relies on tasks never migrating would leave part of the requirement unaddressed, regardless of how it handles cancellation.
What if it supports migration but checks borrows dynamically after a task moves?

That would conflict with the requirement to avoid runtime borrow checks. Migration has to be accounted for without making dynamic borrow validation the basis of the guarantee. The same restriction applies when cancellation is involved.
Does this goal also require proving that every cancelled task promptly releases resources?

The stated guarantee is memory safety under cancellation and migration. It does not additionally specify prompt release, scheduling behavior, or a particular resource-cleanup policy. Those may be important design questions, but they should not be silently substituted for the ownership-checking and program-acceptance requirements here.

Let me check the scope: the design must permit safe borrowed-resource transfers between tasks, statically protect them through cancellation and migration, and make the specified safe-versus-unsafe distinctions.

Yes. More precisely, the goal is an ownership type checker for cancellable asynchronous tasks that safely transfers borrowed resources across task boundaries; guarantees memory safety under cancellation and task migration without whole-program analysis or runtime borrow checks; and accepts 12 safe while rejecting 12 unsafe programs covering nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation.
How would you structure a checker for that goal without relying on whole-program analysis?

I propose a modular region-and-effect checker. Its main pieces would be region-indexed affine task handles, scoped reborrows, Send migration bounds, and cancel-and-join teardown. Together, those give the checker a way to express which borrows a task may retain, how those borrows relate to their sources, what may migrate, and when a task's access has ended. This is a proposed design, not yet a demonstrated safety result.
What does “modular” mean in that proposal?

It means checking a task boundary using the ownership, region, and effect information available at that boundary, rather than needing to inspect every use throughout the whole program. The proposal is to make the obligations visible to the checker locally enough to enforce them without whole-program analysis. The exact form of those interfaces is not specified here.
Why combine regions and effects instead of using only one of them?

They describe different aspects of the problem. Regions express how the validity of a borrow relates to the period during which it can be used. Effects can express relevant aspects of task behavior that the boundary must account for. In the proposal, the checker would use both kinds of information to reason about borrowed resources in cancellable asynchronous tasks; no particular effect vocabulary or formal rule set has been fixed.
Where do region-indexed affine task handles enter the picture?

A region index would connect a task handle to the region obligations associated with the task. Making the handle affine means it cannot be freely duplicated as though each copy independently controlled the same task. The proposal uses that connection to keep outstanding task access visible when reasoning about a borrowed resource. It does not yet specify a concrete type syntax or all the operations permitted on a handle.
Is the idea that dropping a handle automatically makes every borrowed resource available again?

That would be too strong an assumption to make from the proposal. If a task can still use a borrow, merely losing a reference to its handle would not establish that the borrow is finished. The proposed teardown is cancel-and-join: cancellation and confirmation that the task has ended are both relevant before treating its access as over. The detailed rules for handles and teardown still need to be defined.
Could you clarify the difference between cancelling and joining in that phrase?

Cancellation concerns asking the task to stop; joining concerns knowing that it has finished. A cancellation request alone does not establish that no future task use of a borrowed resource is possible. The cancel-and-join proposal makes that distinction part of teardown, without assuming that cancellation is instantaneous or prescribing a particular cancellation mechanism.
How do scoped reborrows help when a borrow crosses into a task?

A scoped reborrow keeps the task's access tied to an existing borrowing relationship and to a defined scope. That matters especially for nested borrows: the checker must not treat a reborrow as an independent right to use the resource after the relationship supporting it has ceased to be valid. The proposal is to represent that dependency rather than regard every cross-task borrow as unrelated to its source.
Does “scoped” mean the asynchronous task has to finish before the scope can end?

The proposed safety reasoning needs the task's possible use of a scoped reborrow to end before the scope that supports it is treated as over. Joining is one way the proposal connects task termination to that reasoning, including when cancellation is requested. Exactly how the checker expresses the scope boundary remains a design detail, so I would not claim a complete rule from the name alone.
What role do Send migration bounds play? Do they make any borrowed resource safe to transfer?

No. Send migration bounds are the proposal's constraint on what may move with a task when migration is possible. They address migration compatibility; they do not erase borrow validity requirements or convert borrowing into ownership. A resource carried across a task boundary still needs the appropriate region and ownership relationships, whether or not it meets a Send bound.
So a migration bound and a region check answer separate questions?

Yes. At a high level, the region side asks whether the task's use of a borrow remains within the period in which that borrow is valid. The Send bound asks whether what the task carries satisfies the migration constraint. Meeting one condition does not imply meeting the other. The proposed checker would need to account for both.
Where does ownership transfer fit if the proposal emphasizes reborrowing?

Scoped reborrows cover borrowed access; ownership transfer is a distinct case the checker must also distinguish. The affine-handle and region-and-effect approach is proposed as a structure for tracking task-related obligations without conflating a transferred owner with a borrower. The proposal does not yet give detailed transfer rules, so it would be premature to say precisely which ownership-transfer programs it accepts.
Would the checker be making runtime decisions about whether those borrows are still valid?

No runtime borrow checks are part of this proposal. The intended ownership and region obligations are checked statically. Task execution, cancellation, and joining are runtime events, but their occurrence is not meant to replace a static check of whether a borrow is permissible.
Can you walk through a general cancellation situation without inventing a specific program?

Conceptually, suppose a task can use a scoped reborrow and cancellation is requested while that task remains outstanding. The checker must not reason as though the borrow became unavailable to the task at the instant of the request. Under the proposed cancel-and-join teardown, joining supplies the relevant confirmation that task access has ended before the supporting scope can be treated as free of that task's use. This illustrates the intended relationship, not a fully specified operational rule.
And if that same task can migrate?

The migration possibility adds the Send-bound obligation for what the task carries. It does not shorten the reborrow's required validity or make cancel-and-join unnecessary. The proposed pieces address the concerns together: region and scoped-reborrow information for borrowed access, a migration bound for what moves, and teardown that does not confuse requesting cancellation with confirmed completion.
How would we know whether this proposal is sufficiently permissive rather than simply prohibiting borrowed tasks?

It would need to accept the 12 safe programs while rejecting the 12 unsafe programs, with coverage of nested borrows, ownership transfer, and cancellation. Those are evaluation requirements inherited from the goal. The proposal describes a checker structure intended to meet them; it does not claim that the program outcomes have already been established.
So the proposal is a particular combination of mechanisms, but the exact typing judgments and outcomes remain to be worked out?

Exactly. The proposed combination is a modular region-and-effect checker with region-indexed affine task handles, scoped reborrows, Send migration bounds, and cancel-and-join teardown. Its purpose is to support a static memory-safety argument for borrowed resources across cancellable, migratable task boundaries without whole-program analysis or runtime borrow checks. Formal rules and results for the required safe and unsafe programs are not specified by the proposal itself.
What handle-region rule would reject detaching a task with borrowed captures while still permitting moved-owned captures to outlive the spawning scope?

A candidate rule is to index a task handle by every region on which the task’s captures depend. A handle for a task with a borrowed capture remains constrained by that borrow’s region; it cannot be detached, because detaching would let the task continue without an obligation to establish that its use of the borrow has ended. For detach, require that the task have no borrowed captures or other borrowed-region dependencies. Moving owned captures into the task need not tie the handle to the spawning scope, so the task may outlive that scope if its captures satisfy the other applicable requirements, including Send bounds when migration is possible.
What exactly does the handle’s region index represent in that rule?

It represents an obligation associated with the task’s possible access to captured resources. If a captured borrow is valid only within a region, the task must not be allowed to keep using it after that region ends. The handle carries the region constraint so checking the task does not depend on searching the whole program for its eventual uses.
Why put the constraint on the handle instead of only checking that the borrow was valid when the task was spawned?

Validity at spawning is not enough: the asynchronous task may use the capture later. A region-indexed handle keeps the outstanding task tied to the period in which its borrowed captures must remain valid. Detaching would discard that connection while leaving the task able to continue, which is the situation the proposed rule rejects.
Does the rule mean an affine handle can never be transferred?

No. Affinity prevents treating duplicated handles as independent rights over one task; it does not by itself prohibit moving the handle. If a handle is moved, its borrowed-region constraints must move with it. Transferring the handle must not turn a task with borrowed captures into a detachable one or extend the validity of those borrows.
How does cancel-and-join teardown fit when the handle has a borrowed-region constraint?

It provides a way to end the task’s possible access before the supporting borrow region is treated as finished. A cancellation request alone is not confirmation that the task has stopped using its captures; joining establishes completion. The handle-region rule can therefore require that an outstanding borrowed task be brought to a point where its access has ended, rather than allowing its handle to be detached.
Would you permit detachment if a borrowed capture happened to remain valid for a very long time?

For the rule you asked for—one that rejects detaching tasks with borrowed captures—the detach condition should test for borrowed captures, not merely guess that a particular borrow will last long enough. A long-lived borrow is still a borrowed capture. Keeping the condition explicit also avoids conflating borrow validity with permission to abandon the task handle.
Then why is moving an owned value different? The task can still keep using it after the spawning scope ends.

Because the move transfers the owned value to the task rather than leaving the task dependent on a borrow from the spawning scope. The spawning scope need not remain active solely to support that ownership. This permission is conditional: a supposedly owned capture must not hide a borrowed-region dependency that expires with the spawning scope, and any required migration bound must still hold.
So the rule cannot just look at whether the outermost capture is labelled owned?

Correct. It must account for the dependencies of what the task captures. Moving ownership of a value does not make any borrow contained within it valid for longer. The intended distinction is between captures that genuinely have no relevant borrowed-region dependence and captures whose use still relies on a borrow.
What happens with a scoped reborrow used as the task capture?

The task’s access would remain tied to the reborrow’s scope and to the borrowing relationship supporting it. Its handle would retain that region constraint, so detach would be rejected. The reborrow must not become an independent, longer-lived right merely because it crossed a task boundary.
Is the Send bound what allows a moved-owned task to outlive the spawning scope?

It answers a separate question. A moved-owned capture avoids dependence on the spawning scope’s borrow region only if it contains no such borrowed dependency. A Send bound addresses whether what the task carries satisfies the constraint for migration. If the task may migrate, both considerations matter; Send does not lengthen a borrow, and ownership alone does not establish migration compatibility.
Can the detach condition be stated compactly?

As a proposed condition: permit detach only when the task’s captured state has no borrowed-region obligations that require retaining its handle; otherwise reject detach and keep the handle subject to those obligations until task access has ended. A moved-owned capture can pass that condition when it has no such dependency, even if the task continues beyond the spawning scope. This states the intended distinction without fixing a particular type-rule notation.
Does that depend on a runtime check at the point of detachment?

No. Whether the captured state carries borrowed-region obligations is a static ownership and region question. The checker would reject a detach operation on a handle with those obligations. Runtime task completion still matters to cancel-and-join teardown, but runtime borrow checking is not the basis of the detach rule.
So the key is that detaching cannot erase a borrowed task’s region obligations, while moving ownership can remove dependence on the spawning scope without erasing any actual borrows?

Yes. That is the distinction the proposed handle-region rule needs to preserve. It rejects detach for borrowed captures, carries region obligations with an affine handle while the task is outstanding, and allows a task with genuinely moved-owned captures to outlive its spawning scope when no borrowed dependency or applicable migration constraint prevents it.

I have a hypothesis for the handle-region rule: require detached captures to be owned, Send, and 'static, while requiring region-bounded cancel-and-join for scoped borrows. That should classify all 24 BorrowTask cases.

That is a clear hypothesis addressing the detach question. The proposed distinction is that a detached task cannot depend on a borrow tied to the spawning scope: its captures must be owned and satisfy both Send and 'static. A task carrying a scoped borrow instead remains bounded by the borrow’s region and uses cancel-and-join teardown. Whether these conditions actually classify all 24 BorrowTask cases remains to be established.
Why require all three conditions for detached captures? Aren’t owned and 'static saying the same thing?

They answer different questions. Ownership says the capture is transferred rather than merely borrowed from the spawning scope. The 'static condition rules out a shorter-lived borrowed dependency within what was transferred; moving ownership of a container would not, by itself, extend the validity of a borrow inside it. Send is the separate migration condition. The hypothesis requires all three for detachment.
Does 'static mean the detached task or its captures must exist forever?

No. In this context, 'static is a restriction on borrowed lifetime dependencies, not a claim that the task runs forever or that its owned values can never be destroyed. The point is that detachment must not leave the task relying on a borrow that expires with a shorter scope.
How does that allow moved-owned captures to outlive the spawning scope?

If a capture is genuinely moved into the task and meets the Send+'static conditions, its continued use need not depend on the spawning scope remaining active. The hypothesis therefore permits detachment in that situation. Calling a capture “moved-owned” is not enough if it still contains a shorter-lived borrow: the 'static condition must apply to the captured state, not just its outer label.
And a direct borrowed capture would fail the detached-capture condition?

A scoped borrowed capture would not meet the hypothesis’s requirement that detached captures be owned and 'static. Rather than allowing that task to detach, the proposed alternative is to keep its use within the relevant region and perform cancel-and-join teardown. That is the intended rejection of detaching borrowed captures, not a measured outcome for a particular BorrowTask case.
What work is the region bound doing in the scoped-borrow branch?

It ties the task’s possible use of the borrow to the period in which that borrow is valid. The task must not remain able to use the scoped borrow after its supporting region has ended. The hypothesis pairs that bound with cancel-and-join so that asking a task to stop is not mistaken for knowing its access has stopped.
Would cancellation on its own satisfy the proposed scoped-borrow rule?

No. The hypothesis specifically says cancel-and-join. Cancellation requests that the task stop; joining establishes that the task has ended. For a scoped borrow, a request alone would not establish that the task can no longer access the borrowed resource before its region ends.
Is Send doing anything for scoped borrows, or is it only mentioned for detachment?

The explicit Send+'static requirement in this hypothesis is for detached captures. The broader design still has Send migration bounds, so migration cannot simply be ignored for a task carrying a scoped borrow. The hypothesis does not spell out a separate complete rule for such migration; it states the detach condition and the region-bounded cancel-and-join condition for scoped borrows.
Does this amount to saying that every asynchronous task must have 'static captures?

No. The proposed 'static requirement applies to detached captures. Scoped borrows are the contrasting case: they may have a bounded region, provided the task’s access is kept within that region through the proposed cancel-and-join arrangement. Applying the detach condition to every task would erase that distinction.
What exactly does “classify all 24 BorrowTask cases” assert here?

It is a predicted outcome for the complete set of 24 BorrowTask cases, not a report that they have been checked. In light of the goal’s 12 safe and 12 unsafe programs, the desired classification is to accept the safe cases and reject the unsafe cases. The hypothesis says these conditions should suffice; it does not provide the cases or their observed results.
Could we already call the memory-safety guarantee proved if the conditions sound right?

Not on that basis alone. The conditions describe a proposed static distinction between detached owned captures and region-bounded borrowed captures. A memory-safety guarantee under cancellation and task migration would still need a sound account of how those conditions are enforced. The claim about all 24 BorrowTask cases is likewise a hypothesis until their classifications are established.

I want to be precise: the detached branch requires owned Send+'static captures, and the scoped-borrow branch requires region-bounded cancel-and-join. Neither branch gets to treat cancellation as instantaneous.

Yes. That states the hypothesis without turning it into a result. Detachment is reserved for captures meeting owned Send+'static; scoped borrows remain bounded by their regions and use cancel-and-join. Joining matters because cancellation alone does not establish that a task has stopped accessing its captures. The open claim is that this distinction should classify all 24 BorrowTask cases.
Let’s implement a checker prototype and run BorrowTask’s 12 safe and 12 unsafe cases across nested reborrows, detach, cancellation, and migration.

That activity would put the proposed rules to a concrete test. The prototype should apply the ownership, region, and task conditions to BorrowTask’s 24 cases: 12 designated safe and 12 designated unsafe. The run should cover nested reborrows, detach, cancellation, and migration. No classification results are specified yet.
Which hypothesis is this run evaluating?

It evaluates the hypothesis that requiring owned Send+'static captures for detached tasks and region-bounded cancel-and-join for scoped borrows should classify all 24 BorrowTask cases. Running the cases would test that prediction; the activity alone does not establish that the prediction holds.
Why include nested reborrows rather than testing only direct borrows captured by tasks?

Nested reborrows exercise whether the checker preserves the borrowing relationships on which a task’s access depends. A direct-borrow case alone would not cover that aspect of the stated case set. The activity calls for running the cases across nested reborrows, without specifying any particular case’s code or expected diagnostic.
What is detach meant to exercise in the prototype?

It exercises the distinction between a task that may continue independently and one whose captures still depend on a scoped borrow. The proposed rule requires detached captures to be owned Send+'static. The run is meant to test how the prototype classifies BorrowTask’s detach cases, not to assume their outcomes in advance.
And what should the cancellation cases tell us?

They should exercise the proposed treatment of scoped borrows when a task is cancelled, particularly the distinction between requesting cancellation and establishing completion through cancel-and-join. The requirement is to run the cancellation cases and compare the checker’s classifications with their safe or unsafe designations; no observed behavior is given here.
Migration is listed separately. Shouldn’t a correct region rule already cover it?

Region constraints address the validity of borrowed access; migration also raises the Send-bound condition for what a task carries. Running BorrowTask’s migration cases is therefore part of evaluating the proposed checker, rather than assuming that checking regions alone settles migration.
Do we need 12 safe and 12 unsafe cases for each of those four areas?

No per-area count is stated. The activity specifies BorrowTask’s 12 safe and 12 unsafe cases in total, across nested reborrows, detach, cancellation, and migration. It does not specify how many cases belong to each area or whether an individual case covers more than one.
When you say “run” them, are you claiming the checker has already accepted or rejected any of the cases?

No. Implementing the prototype and running the cases describes the activity. This node supplies no results, so it would be premature to report how many cases the prototype accepts or rejects, or whether any classification agrees with the safe and unsafe designations.
What would we compare once the prototype produces classifications?

For each of BorrowTask’s 12 designated safe and 12 designated unsafe cases, the relevant comparison is the prototype’s acceptance or rejection against that designation. That comparison would bear on the hypothesis about all 24 cases. At this stage, it remains a comparison to perform, not a finding.
So the immediate work is the prototype and the full BorrowTask run, while leaving conclusions about the hypothesis open?

Exactly. Implement the checker prototype and run all 24 BorrowTask cases—12 safe and 12 unsafe—covering nested reborrows, detach, cancellation, and migration. The activity evaluates the proposed detach and scoped-borrow rules, but it does not itself report a classification result or a memory-safety proof.
What did the BorrowTask v0.1 run show?
BorrowTask v0.1 accepted 12/12 safe cases and rejected 12/12 unsafe cases. The cases covered reborrows, cancellation, detachment, and migration.
So did any of the designated safe cases get rejected?
No. The reported result is 12 accepted out of 12 designated safe cases. Likewise, all 12 designated unsafe cases were rejected.
Is that 12 cases for each of the four topics?
No. The result covers 12 safe and 12 unsafe cases in total, across reborrows, cancellation, detachment, and migration. It does not give a separate count for each topic.
Does “rejected 12/12 unsafe” tell us why each case was rejected?

It reports the classifications, not the individual reasons or diagnostics. We can say that BorrowTask v0.1 rejected every case designated unsafe in this run, but the result does not identify which rule was decisive for any particular case.
How should I describe the outcome without overstating it?

Say that BorrowTask v0.1 accepted all 12 designated safe cases and rejected all 12 designated unsafe cases in the reported set, which covered reborrows, cancellation, detachment, and migration. That is a precise account of the result. It does not, by itself, establish how the checker would classify programs outside those 24 cases.
Does the run prove memory safety under cancellation and task migration?

The reported classifications are test evidence, not a memory-safety proof. They show that BorrowTask v0.1 made the specified acceptance and rejection distinctions on these 24 cases, including cases concerning cancellation and migration. A general guarantee for all programs would require more than these case results alone.
Can I infer that the checker needed neither whole-program analysis nor runtime borrow checks from those numbers?

Not from the numbers alone. The 12/12 and 12/12 figures report which cases were accepted and rejected. They do not describe the analysis the checker performed or whether it used runtime borrow checks. Those design requirements should be assessed separately from the reported case classifications.
What about the detach distinction we discussed—does this result identify which detach cases had borrowed captures?

No individual detach cases or captures are described in the result. It says that detachment was among the areas covered and reports the aggregate safe and unsafe classifications. Assigning a particular capture pattern or outcome to a particular case would go beyond that evidence.
Could all the migration cases have been safe, or all unsafe?

The aggregate report does not give the migration cases’ safe-versus-unsafe breakdown. It establishes that migration was covered, but not how many migration cases had either designation or what happened in each one individually.
Is it fair to say there were no classification errors in the reported set?

Yes, with the set clearly identified: on the 24 reported BorrowTask v0.1 cases, all 12 designated safe cases were accepted and all 12 designated unsafe cases were rejected. That says nothing about unreported cases or other versions of the checker.
I want the wording to preserve both the version and the exact denominators.
Then state it directly: “BorrowTask v0.1 accepted 12/12 safe cases and rejected 12/12 unsafe cases across reborrows, cancellation, detachment, and migration.”
I’m ready to adopt the handle-region rule for scoped borrows and require owned Send+'static captures for detachment. BorrowTask passed all 24 cases.

That states the decision and its reported basis precisely. Scoped borrows remain subject to the handle-region rule, while detach is permitted only for captures that are owned, Send, and 'static. BorrowTask passed all 24 cases. The case result supports adopting the rule, though it should not be described as a proof of memory safety for every possible program.
What is the essential obligation on a handle for a task carrying a scoped borrow?

The handle must retain the region obligation associated with the task’s possible use of that borrow. The task cannot be treated as independent of the region that supports its captured access. Under the adopted rule, the handle remains constrained until the task’s access has ended within that region.
Does adoption mean a scoped-borrow task can never be spawned?

No. The distinction is between allowing a scoped-borrow task while preserving its region obligation and detaching it so it could continue without that obligation. The handle-region rule is intended to permit the former when its constraints are met, not to ban all borrowed captures.
How should teardown be understood for such a task?

In the scoped-borrow arrangement we have been discussing, cancel-and-join keeps a cancellation request distinct from confirmation that the task has ended. The region obligation cannot be discharged merely by asking the task to stop while it might still access the borrow. The adopted handle-region rule preserves that constraint.
Why not make an exception to detachment for a borrowed capture that seems likely to remain available?

The adopted detach condition is owned Send+'static captures, not a prediction that a particular borrow will remain available. A scoped borrow continues to carry its region dependency. Treating an expectation about its duration as permission to detach would bypass the distinction the decision establishes.
If I move a value into a detached task, is being the owner sufficient?

Not by itself. The decision requires the detached captures to be owned, Send, and 'static. An owned value could still carry a shorter-lived borrowed dependency, so the 'static condition matters; Send addresses the migration constraint. The conditions apply to what the task captures, not just to the fact that a move occurred.
Does 'static say that the detached task must run indefinitely?

No. It constrains lifetime dependencies of the captured state; it does not specify how long the task runs. Its role here is to keep detachment from relying on a borrow whose supporting scope may end while the task remains active.
And Send does not replace the region rule?

Correct. Send addresses whether captured state satisfies the migration bound. It does not extend the validity of a scoped borrow. A task with borrowed captures remains subject to the handle-region rule even if migration is also relevant.
What, exactly, does the BorrowTask outcome let us say in support of the decision?

It lets us say that BorrowTask passed all 24 cases under the reported evaluation. That is the case-based support for adopting this rule. It does not provide individual case details in the decision statement or establish that every program outside those cases will be classified correctly.
Should I describe the rule as a proven guarantee under both cancellation and migration?

I would keep the claims separate. The decision is to adopt the handle-region rule for scoped borrows and owned Send+'static captures for detach, and the reported BorrowTask outcome is that all 24 cases passed. A general memory-safety proof under cancellation and migration is a broader claim than that case result alone establishes.
Can I at least say that the adopted distinction is meant to prevent detachment from erasing a borrow obligation?

Yes. That is the purpose of the distinction: a scoped borrow keeps its region obligation through the task handle, whereas detachment requires captures that meet owned Send+'static. The wording describes what the rule requires without claiming an unreported proof.
Give me a concise decision statement I can use.
Adopt the handle-region rule for tasks with scoped borrows and require owned Send+'static captures for detached tasks. BorrowTask passed all 24 cases.
What should we do next for the adopted handle-region rule?

The plan is to prove compositional preservation and progress for the adopted handle-region rule and cancel-and-join teardown under migration, and to expand BorrowTask transfer regressions. Those are planned tasks, not completed proofs or new regression results.
Why do we need a proof if we can run more BorrowTask cases?
